title: Unit 5e - Polymorphism
summary: Title slide introducing the Polymorphism unit for CS103, taught by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: Unit 5e - Polymorphism. Instructor: Mark Redekopp. Opening title slide for the polymorphism unit in CS103.
notes_text: This unit builds directly on Unit 5d (Inheritance) and introduces the concept of polymorphism, virtual functions, and abstract classes.

title: So, When Should We Use Inheritance
summary: Reviews two reasons to use inheritance: extending base class functionality and enabling polymorphic behavior in hierarchies.
main_text: Reason 1: When you want the full interface of the base class but just add or extend functionality. Example: class ReversibleString : public std::string. You get all the other string functions 'for free' and can write only the extended functionality, such as a void reverse() method. In main(), a ReversibleString s1("Hello") can use s1.size() (returns 5), s1[0] (returns 'H'), s1.substr(3) (returns "lo"), and the new s1.reverse() followed by cout << s1 outputs "olleH". Reason 2: When you have a hierarchy of related objects, want to enforce common interfaces, and/or use POLYMORPHIC behavior. More on this in this unit.
notes_text: This slide is repeated from Unit 5d to bridge into polymorphism. Reason 2 is the focus of this entire unit. Polymorphism is arguably the most important reason to use inheritance in practice.

images.description: Code example showing ReversibleString class inheriting from std::string, adding only a reverse() method, with main function demonstrating inherited string methods alongside the new reverse method.

title: Coupling
summary: Defines coupling as dependency between components, contrasting low coupling (good) with tight coupling (bad), and how OO design reduces it.
main_text: Coupling refers to how much components depend on each other's implementation details (i.e. how much work it is to remove one component and drop in a new implementation of it). Low coupling (good) vs. Tight coupling (not so good): Replacing a new battery in your car (low coupling) vs. Replacing a new engine in your car (tight coupling). Adding a USB device to your laptop (low coupling) vs. Replacing the CPU in your laptop (tight coupling). OO Design seeks to reduce coupling as much as possible by creating well-defined interfaces to update (write) or access (read) the state of an object, and allowing alternate implementations that do NOT require interface changes.
notes_text: Coupling is a fundamental software engineering concept that motivates both encapsulation and polymorphism. Low coupling means you can swap implementations without changing the code that uses them. This is exactly what virtual functions and abstract classes achieve.

title: Polymorphism - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing the polymorphism topic.
main_text: Polymorphism. This section introduces the core concept of polymorphism: using the same expression to operate on different types with different behavior for each type.
notes_text: Polymorphism literally means 'many forms.' In C++, it is achieved through virtual functions and inheritance, allowing a single interface to operate on objects of different derived types.

title: Base and Derived Type Compatibility
summary: Explains that a derived object can be assigned to a base object (slicing), but not vice versa, using animal classification analogy.
main_text: Are base and derived objects type compatible? Can we assign a derived object into a base object? Can we assign a base object into a derived? Consider: p = s (Base = Derived) and s = p (Derived = Base). Think hierarchy and animal classification: Can any dog be (assigned as) a mammal? Yes. Can any mammal be (assigned as) a dog? No. We can only assign a derived into a base (since the derived has EVERYTHING the base does). p = s is valid (Base = Derived is Good). s = p is invalid (Derived = Base is Bad). The memory layout shows Person has name_ and id_, while Student has name_, id_, major_, and gpa_. Assigning Student to Person copies only name_ and id_ (object slicing).
notes_text: This is the foundation for understanding pointer/reference compatibility. The key principle: a derived IS a base, so you can always treat a derived as a base. But a base is NOT necessarily a derived, so the reverse is unsafe. Object slicing occurs when assigning a derived to a base by value - the derived-specific members are lost.

images.description: Memory layout diagrams for Class Person (name_, id_) and Class Student (name_, id_, major_, gpa_) with arrows showing valid assignment direction from Student to Person and a prohibition symbol on the reverse direction.

title: Pointer and Reference Compatibility
summary: Establishes that base-type pointers/references CAN point to derived objects, but derived pointers CANNOT point to base or sibling objects.
main_text: Important fact: A base-type pointer (or reference) CAN point at (reference) a derived object. The compiler will see a pointer or reference to a derived class object is type-compatible with (can be assigned to) a base-class type pointer/reference. Example: Derived d; Base* b = &d; is valid. But not vice versa. A derived class pointer or reference CANNOT point to or reference a Base object. Base b; Derived* d = &b; is invalid. And clearly a derived pointer or reference is NOT type compatible with a different derived type pointer/reference. In the code: Person *q; q = &p (ok), q = &s (ok), q = &f (ok). But Student *t = &p (not ok), Faculty *g = &s (not ok). Base pointer CAN point at any publicly derived object. Derived pointer CANNOT point at base or sibling objects.
notes_text: This is the mechanism that makes polymorphism possible. Because a base pointer can point to any derived object, we can write code that uses base pointers and have it work with any derived type. This is the key enabler for virtual function dispatch.

images.description: Diagram showing a Person* q pointer with arrows to three objects: P (Person), S (Student with P inside), and F (Faculty with P inside). Green checkmarks show valid pointer assignments, red X marks show invalid ones. A separate Student* t pointer shows it cannot point to P or F objects.
labels: Base pointer CAN point at any publicly derived object
Derived pointer CANNOT point at base or sibling objects

title: Think About Ability
summary: Explains why base pointers can safely point to derived objects: derived objects guarantee they can do everything a base can do.
main_text: Is it a guarantee that a Student or Faculty object can do anything a Person object can? Yes, because each inherited the Person class. So, we can treat any Student or Faculty as we would a Person. Is it a guarantee that a Person can do anything Student or Faculty can do? No! Inheritance enforces and provides guarantees on what certain objects can do. This is why base pointers can safely reference derived objects: the derived object is guaranteed to support all base operations.
notes_text: This slide provides the logical justification for pointer compatibility. The guarantee flows downward: derived classes inherit all base capabilities. But it does not flow upward: base classes do not have derived-specific capabilities. This guarantee is what makes polymorphism type-safe.

images.description: Diagram showing Person* q pointer pointing to three nested objects (P, S containing P, F containing P), each with a print_info() method. Dashed lines show the pointer can reach any of these objects.

title: Which Function Gets Called?
summary: Poses the question of which overloaded function version is called when using a base pointer to a derived object, introducing static binding.
main_text: Since a Student or Faculty can do ANYTHING a Person can do, we can point a base class pointer at the Derived object and call Person member functions on a Student and/or Faculty. But what happens if both base and derived overload a function? Which version gets called? The default approach is to always apply the function from the class corresponding to the pointer type being used. In the code: Person *q; q = &p; q->print_info() prints Name=Bill, ID=1. q = &s; q->print_info() prints Name=Joe, ID=2. q = &f; q->print_info() prints Name=Ken, ID=3. All three calls use Person::print_info() because the pointer type is Person*.
notes_text: This slide sets up the problem that virtual functions solve. Without virtual, the compiler uses static binding based on the pointer type, not the object type. So even though q points to a Student, Person::print_info() is called because q is a Person*. This is not the desired behavior when we want derived-specific output.

images.description: Diagram showing Person* q pointer with dashed arrows to P, S, and F objects, each with their own print_info() method. The question mark indicates uncertainty about which version is called.

title: Non-Virtual Functions: Base Pointer => Base Functions (Static Binding)
summary: Explains static binding: without virtual, a base pointer always calls the base class version of an overloaded function.
main_text: For the second and third calls to print_info() we might like to have Student::print_info() and Faculty::print_info() executed since the actual object pointed to is a Student/Faculty. BUT it will call Person::print_info(). This is called 'static binding' (i.e. the version of the function called is based on the static type of the pointer being used). With no VIRTUAL declaration in the base class, only the base version from the POINTER TYPE can be called. Output for all three calls is just Name and ID, even when pointing to Student or Faculty objects: Name=Bill, ID=1; Name=Joe, ID=2; Name=Ken, ID=3.
notes_text: Static binding is the default in C++. The compiler determines which function to call at compile time based on the declared type of the pointer/reference. This is efficient but does not support polymorphic behavior. The next slide introduces the virtual keyword that enables dynamic binding.

images.description: Diagram showing Person* q with arrows to P, S, and F objects. Annotations show (1) No VIRTUAL declaration and (2) only the base version from the POINTER TYPE can be called. Output shows all calls produce Person-level output only.

title: Virtual Functions: Dynamic Binding
summary: Introduces the virtual keyword enabling dynamic binding, where the function called is determined by the actual object type, not the pointer type.
main_text: Member functions can be declared virtual. The virtual declaration allows derived classes to redefine the function, and which version is called is determined by the type of object pointed to/referenced rather than the type of the pointer/reference. Note: You do NOT have to override a virtual function in the derived class; you can just inherit and use the base class version. This is called 'dynamic binding' (i.e. which version is called is based on the type of object being pointed to). With virtual void print_info() in Person, the output now shows: Name=Bill, ID=1 (Person object); Name=Joe, ID=2, Major=5 (Student object); Name=Mary, ID=3, Tenured=1 (Faculty object).
notes_text: The virtual keyword is the single most important mechanism for polymorphism in C++. Adding 'virtual' to the base class function declaration changes the dispatch mechanism from static (compile-time) to dynamic (run-time). The compiler generates a virtual table (vtable) that enables this runtime dispatch.

images.description: Diagram showing Person* q pointing to P, S, and F objects. With VIRTUAL declaration in base class, arrows now go to each object's own print_info() implementation. Output shows type-specific information for each object.

title: Polymorphism
summary: Demonstrates polymorphism with an array of base pointers storing different derived types, each calling its own print_info via virtual dispatch.
main_text: Can we have an array that stores multiple types (e.g. an array that stores both ints and doubles)? NO!! But we can use base pointers to point at different types and have their individual behavior invoked via virtual functions. Polymorphism via virtual functions allows one set of code to operate appropriately on all derived types of objects using each object's individual behaviors! One data structure can now reference many types and the code can perform appropriate behavior on each as you iterate over the structure. Example: Person* p[5]; p[0] = new Person("Bill",1); p[1] = new Student("Joe",2,5); p[2] = new Faculty("Ken",3,0); p[3] = new Student("Mary",4,2); p[4] = new Faculty("Jen",5,1); A single for loop calling p[i]->print_info() prints type-specific info for each object.
notes_text: This is the canonical example of polymorphism. A single array of Person* can store pointers to Person, Student, and Faculty objects. A single loop iterates over all of them, and each call to print_info() automatically dispatches to the correct version based on the actual object type. This is the power of polymorphism: uniform code that handles diverse types.

images.description: Diagram showing a Person* p[5] array of pointers, each pointing to different objects: a P (Person), two S (Student) objects, and two F (Faculty) objects. Each object is shown as a circle with its type letter inside.

title: Polymorphic Hierarchies
summary: Notes that virtual persists through the hierarchy, child classes can add new virtual functions, and derived classes may inherit virtual implementations.
main_text: A few notes about polymorphic hierarchies: Once a function is declared virtual, it is virtual in perpetuity. The keyword virtual need not be repeated in child or grandchild classes. A child/grandchild cannot 'unvirtualize' the function. Child classes can create additional virtual functions that apply (e.g. Student::study()). A child class need NOT provide their own implementation of a virtual function if they are happy with the implementation they will inherit (see CSStudent::print_info() which inherits Student's version). Example hierarchy: Person has virtual print_info() and non-virtual code(). Student overrides print_info(), adds virtual code() and virtual study(). CSStudent overrides code() and study() but inherits Student::print_info().
notes_text: Key takeaways: (1) virtual is inherited automatically, (2) new virtual functions can be introduced at any level, (3) not every derived class must override every virtual function. This flexibility allows hierarchies to grow organically without forcing unnecessary reimplementation.

title: Polymorphism: As Easy as 1-2-3
summary: Provides a three-step algorithm for determining which function gets called: check pointer type, check if virtual, then resolve based on binding type.
main_text: Step 1: Determine what type of pointer/reference is being used to call the function. Step 2: Go to the prototype of the function in the class that matches the type of pointer/reference and ask: 'Is it virtual?' at that level in the hierarchy. Step 3a: If no, execute the function from the class matching the pointer type (static binding). Step 3b: If yes, execute the function from the class matching the type of object being pointed to or referenced (dynamic binding). This three-step process works for any polymorphic call in any inheritance hierarchy.
notes_text: This is the definitive algorithm students should memorize for exams. The critical insight is that the pointer type determines WHERE to look for the virtual keyword, and the virtual keyword determines WHETHER to use the object type (dynamic) or pointer type (static) for dispatch.

title: Pointers, References, and Objects
summary: Clarifies that dynamic binding requires base class pointers or references; copying a derived to a base object causes slicing with no polymorphism.
main_text: To allow dynamic binding and polymorphism the base class must specify the function as virtual AND then use a base class Pointer or Reference to the derived objects. Three functions demonstrate: f1(Person* p) uses a pointer and calls Student::print_info() via dynamic binding. f2(const Person& p) uses a reference and also calls Student::print_info() via dynamic binding. f3(Person p) takes a Person by value, which copies (slices) the Student into a Person, so Person::print_info() is called on the copy - no polymorphic behavior is possible! Output: f1(&s) prints Name=Joe, ID=2, Major=5. f2(s) prints Name=Joe, ID=2, Major=5. f3(s) prints Name=Joe, ID=2 (sliced, no major).
notes_text: This is a common pitfall. Passing by value creates a copy of only the base portion of the object (object slicing). The derived-specific data and behavior are lost. Always use pointers or references when you need polymorphic behavior. This is why function parameters for polymorphic types should always be pointers or references.

images.description: Diagram showing Person and Student memory layouts. Blue arrows from f1 (pointer) and f2 (reference) point to the full Student object. f3 (by value) creates a sliced Person copy, losing the Student-specific members.

title: Summary: Static vs Dynamic Binding
summary: Summarizes the difference: without virtual, binding is static (based on pointer type); with virtual, binding is dynamic (based on object type).
main_text: No virtual declaration: Member function that is called is based on the type of the pointer/reference. This is Static Binding. With virtual declaration: Member function that is called is based on the type of the object pointed at (referenced). This is Dynamic Binding.
notes_text: This concise summary captures the entire mechanism of polymorphism in C++. Static binding is resolved at compile time and is the default. Dynamic binding is resolved at runtime and requires the virtual keyword. Both have their uses: static binding is faster, dynamic binding is more flexible.

title: Abstract Classes and Pure Virtuals
summary: Introduces pure virtual functions (= 0) and abstract base classes that define interfaces derived classes must implement.
main_text: In software development we may want to create a base class that serves only as a requirement/interface that derived classes must implement and adhere to. Example: Suppose we want to create a CollegeStudent class and ensure all derived objects implement the student's behavior. But depending on which college you go to, you may do these activities differently. Until we know the university, we don't know how to implement take_test() and play_sports(). We can decide to NOT implement them in this class, known as 'pure' virtual functions (indicated by setting their prototype = 0). Syntax: virtual void take_test() = 0; virtual string play_sports() = 0;. A class with 1 or more pure virtuals is called an abstract base class (i.e. interface for future derived classes).
notes_text: Abstract base classes are the C++ equivalent of interfaces in languages like Java. They define a contract that derived classes must fulfill. The = 0 syntax is unique to C++ and tells the compiler this function has no implementation in this class. Any concrete derived class must provide implementations for all pure virtual functions.

images.description: Two code boxes: left shows CollegeStudent with regular virtual functions (can be instantiated), right shows CollegeStudent with pure virtual functions (= 0, abstract, cannot be instantiated). Arrow between them shows the transformation.

title: Abstract Classes and Pure Virtuals - Implementation
summary: Shows TrojanStudent and BruinStudent implementing the abstract CollegeStudent interface with polymorphic dispatch via base pointers.
main_text: An abstract base class is one that defines at least 1 or more pure virtual functions. These are prototype only with function body set to '= 0;'. Functions that are not implemented by the base class but must be implemented by the derived class to be able to create an instance of the derived object. Objects of the abstract class type MAY NOT be declared/instantiated, since some functions are not implemented. Example: CollegeStudent has pure virtuals take_test() = 0 and play_sports() = 0. TrojanStudent implements take_test() { cout << "Got an A."; } and play_sports() { return string("WIN!"); }. BruinStudent implements take_test() { cout << "Uh..uh..C-."; } and play_sports() { return string("LOSE"); }. A vector<CollegeStudent*> can store both types and iterate polymorphically. Output: Got an A. WIN! Uh..uh..C-. LOSE.
notes_text: This example demonstrates the full power of abstract classes: define an interface once, implement it differently in each derived class, and use base pointers to invoke the correct behavior polymorphically. The humorous USC vs UCLA rivalry makes the example memorable.

title: How Long is a Class Abstract?
summary: Explains that a class remains abstract until ALL pure virtual functions have implementations; partial implementation keeps it abstract.
main_text: Objects of the abstract class type MAY NOT be declared/instantiated, because doing so would not be safe since some functions are not implemented. Until each pure virtual function has a definition, the class stays abstract. Example: CollegeStudent has two pure virtuals: take_test() = 0 and play_sports() = 0. TrojanStudent only implements play_sports() but NOT take_test(). Therefore, TrojanStudent is still abstract! CSTrojanStudent inherits from TrojanStudent and implements take_test(). Now CSTrojanStudent has all pure virtuals implemented and CAN be instantiated. CollegeStudent cs1; WON'T COMPILE (abstract). TrojanStudent ts1; WON'T COMPILE (still abstract, missing take_test). Only CSTrojanStudent can be instantiated.
notes_text: This is a subtle but important rule. A derived class inherits the abstract status if it does not implement ALL pure virtual functions. The class hierarchy can spread implementation across multiple levels, but only the first level that completes all implementations becomes concrete (instantiable).

title: Creating Objects of Abstract Classes
summary: Compares a valid class (all functions implemented) with an abstract class (pure virtuals), showing that abstract objects cannot be created.
main_text: We'll see the benefits of abstract classes shortly, but first the restrictions. Objects of an abstract class type cannot be created! Because they are not fully operational. Side-by-side comparison: Left: CollegeStudent with regular virtual functions (virtual void take_test(); virtual string play_sports();) is a valid class and CollegeStudent cs; is fine. Right: CollegeStudent with pure virtual functions (virtual void take_test() = 0; virtual string play_sports() = 0;) is an abstract base class with 2 pure virtual functions. CollegeStudent cs; causes a compile error! No object of type CollegeStudent will be allowed. It only serves as an interface that derived classes will have to implement.
notes_text: The key distinction is the '= 0' suffix. Without it, the functions must have implementations somewhere and the class is concrete. With it, the class becomes abstract and serves purely as an interface specification. You can still declare pointers and references to abstract classes, just not objects.

images.description: Two side-by-side code boxes comparing a valid concrete CollegeStudent class (left, can be instantiated) with an abstract CollegeStudent class (right, causes compile error when instantiated). Pure virtual = 0 syntax highlighted in yellow.

title: When to Use Inheritance
summary: Shows that inheritance with abstract classes allows new derived classes to integrate seamlessly with existing code years later.
main_text: Main use of inheritance is to setup interfaces (abstract classes) that allow for new, derived classes to be written in the future that provide additional functionality but still work seamlessly with original code. Example: A sports_simulator function was compiled 10 years ago with only a CollegeStudent pointer parameter: void sports_simulator(CollegeStudent *stu) { stu->play_sports(); }. Today, a new MITStudent class is written that implements take_test() and play_sports(). The new class works with the existing sports_simulator code without recompilation: the program will run fine today with new MITStudent class because it conforms to the CollegeStudent interface.
notes_text: This is the most compelling argument for inheritance and abstract classes. Code written years ago can work with types that did not exist when it was written, as long as those types conform to the established interface. This is the Open-Closed Principle: open for extension, closed for modification.

title: Abstract Classes - Common Functions and Data
summary: Shows that abstract base classes can still define common functions and data members that all derived classes inherit.
main_text: An abstract base class can still define common functions (e.g. get_color()) and have data members (e.g. 'color' of the Animal). In this way, all derived classes can use these functions and data via inheritance. Example: class Animal has a constructor Animal(string c) : color(c), virtual destructor, string get_color() { return c; }, pure virtual void make_sound() = 0, and protected string color. Dog, Cat, and Fox inherit from Animal and implement make_sound() differently: Dog prints "Bark", Cat prints "Meow", Fox prints "???". In main(), Animal* a[3]; a[0] = new Animal; WON'T COMPILE because Animal is abstract. a[1] = new Dog("brown"); a[2] = new Cat("calico"); cout << a[1]->get_color() outputs "brown". cout << a[2]->make_sound() outputs "meow".
notes_text: This demonstrates that abstract classes are not just empty interfaces. They can contain shared implementation (get_color, color member) that all derived classes inherit. Only the pure virtual functions are left for derived classes to implement. The protected access specifier allows derived classes to access color directly.

title: Inheritance/Polymorphism Example: GUI Components
summary: Real-world example showing a GUI component hierarchy with Component, Window, ListBox, ScrollBox, and DropDownBox.
main_text: A practical example of inheritance and polymorphism in GUI frameworks. Component is the base class with Draw() and onClick() methods. Window inherits from Component and adds Minimize() and Maximize(). ListBox inherits from Component and adds Get_Selection(). ScrollBox inherits from ListBox and adds onScroll(). DropDownBox inherits from ListBox and adds onDropDown(). The inheritance diagram shows arrows from derived to base class relationships. Each component type can be drawn and clicked (inherited from Component), but has specialized behavior for its specific widget type.
notes_text: This is a real-world application of polymorphism. GUI frameworks use inheritance hierarchies exactly like this. A rendering loop can iterate over a collection of Component* and call Draw() on each, with each component rendering itself appropriately. This is polymorphism in production code.

images.description: Inheritance hierarchy diagram showing Component at the top, with Window and ListBox as children. ListBox has two children: ScrollBox and DropDownBox. Arrows point from derived to base. Screenshots of actual ScrollBox (color list) and DropDownBox (file picker) widgets shown below.

title: Example 1 - A Queue Interface
summary: Defines an abstract IntQueue interface with pure virtual functions that different queue implementations must adhere to.
main_text: We have learned that a queue can be implemented using a singly linked list with tail pointer, doubly linked list with tail pointer, and other methods such as a circular array. Let's make a generic Queue interface that can then be inherited by specific implementations. Any derived implementation will have to conform to these public member functions. The IntQueue abstract class defines: virtual bool empty() const = 0; virtual int size() const = 0; virtual void push_back(int new_val) = 0; virtual int front() const = 0; virtual void pop_front() = 0;. All functions are pure virtual (= 0), making IntQueue an abstract base class that serves purely as an interface specification.
notes_text: This is a perfect example of the interface pattern. IntQueue defines WHAT a queue must do, but not HOW. Different implementations can use different data structures internally while conforming to the same interface. This enables polymorphic usage where the caller doesn't need to know which implementation is being used.

title: Example 1 - Derived Implementations
summary: Shows two concrete queue implementations (SLIntQueue and ArrayIntQueue) that inherit from the abstract IntQueue interface.
main_text: Derived implementations can freely implement the queue however they like but MUST adhere to the interface specified by IntQueue. One implementation uses a SINGLY LINKED LIST approach: class SLIntQueue : public IntQueue. It adds to back quickly using the tail pointer and removes from front using the head pointer. Private members: Item* head; Item* tail;. Another implementation uses an array with front and back indices: class ArrayIntQueue : public IntQueue. Private members: int size_, int* arrPtr_, int front_, back_;. Both implementations provide concrete versions of empty(), size(), push_back(), front(), and pop_front() but use completely different internal data structures.
notes_text: This example shows the power of abstract interfaces. Two completely different internal implementations (linked list vs array) present the same public interface. Client code using IntQueue* doesn't need to know or care which implementation is being used.

title: Example 1 - Usage
summary: Demonstrates using base class pointers and references to write implementation-agnostic code that works with any IntQueue.
main_text: Recall that to take advantage of dynamic binding you must use a base-class pointer or reference that points to or references a derived object. The code uses IntQueue* and IntQueue& to write generic functions: void fill_with_data(IntQueue* q) fills any queue implementation with data using q->push_back(i). void print_and_pop(IntQueue& q) prints and removes all items using q.front() and q.pop_front(). In main(): IntQueue* myq = new SLIntQueue; (or SLIntQueue* myq = new SLIntQueue;). fill_with_data(myq); print_and_pop(*myq);. What's the benefit of this approach?
notes_text: The functions fill_with_data and print_and_pop are completely implementation-agnostic. They work with ANY IntQueue implementation. This is the practical benefit of polymorphism: you write code once against the interface, and it works with all current and future implementations.

title: Example 1 - Reduced Coupling and Increased Flexibility
summary: Shows that swapping implementations requires changing only the instantiation line, not any of the algorithmic code.
main_text: What's the benefit of using abstract interfaces? We can drop in a different derived implementation WITHOUT changing any other code other than the instantiation! Years later you can write a new Queue implementation that conforms to the IntQueue interface and drop it in, and the subsystems (e.g. fill_with_data() and print_and_pop()) should work as is. Example: Changing from SLIntQueue to ArrayIntQueue only requires changing one line: IntQueue* myq = new ArrayIntQueue; instead of IntQueue* myq = new SLIntQueue;. The fill_with_data(myq) and print_and_pop(*myq) calls remain unchanged.
notes_text: This demonstrates reduced coupling in practice. The only coupling between the main code and the specific queue implementation is the single 'new' statement. Everything else uses the IntQueue interface. This is sometimes called the Dependency Inversion Principle: depend on abstractions, not concretions.

title: Virtual Destructors [1]
summary: Explains why classes with virtual functions need virtual destructors to avoid memory leaks when deleting through base pointers.
main_text: Classes that have at least 1 virtual function should have a virtual destructor. Problem: class Student has a non-virtual destructor ~Student() { }. class StudentWithGrades : public Student allocates dynamic memory: grades = new int[10]; and its destructor does delete [] grades;. In main(): Student *s = new StudentWithGrades(...); delete s; - Which destructor gets called? Due to static binding (no virtual declaration on destructor), ~Student() gets called and doesn't delete the grades array. This causes a memory leak! The dynamically allocated grades array is never freed.
notes_text: This is a critical rule in C++: if a class has any virtual functions, its destructor must also be virtual. Without a virtual destructor, deleting a derived object through a base pointer will only call the base destructor, potentially leaking resources allocated by the derived class.

images.description: Diagram showing a Student pointer pointing to a StudentWithGrades object which has a pointer to a dynamically allocated grades array. Without virtual destructor, deleting through the base pointer misses the grades array cleanup.

title: Virtual Destructors - Solution
summary: Shows the fix: declaring the base destructor as virtual ensures the correct derived destructor is called through base pointers.
main_text: Classes that have at least 1 virtual function should have a virtual destructor. Solution: Make the base class destructor virtual: virtual ~Student() { }. Now when delete s is called through a Student* pointer, due to dynamic binding (virtual declaration), ~StudentWithGrades() gets called first, which properly deletes the grades array, and then ~Student() is called automatically (destructor chaining). The left side shows the problem (non-virtual destructor, memory leak) and the right side shows the solution (virtual destructor, proper cleanup).
notes_text: Rule of thumb: if you have even one virtual function in a class, make the destructor virtual too. Some coding standards require this unconditionally. The cost of a virtual destructor is minimal (one vtable entry), but the cost of forgetting it can be a hard-to-debug memory leak.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison: left shows non-virtual destructor with broken arrow (memory leak), right shows virtual destructor with correct arrow chain through both destructors. The grades array is properly freed on the right.

title: Review Questions - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing review questions for polymorphism concepts.
main_text: Review Questions. This section provides practice problems for determining which functions get called in polymorphic hierarchies.
notes_text: The following slides test the three-step polymorphism algorithm and understanding of abstract classes, virtual functions, and binding types.

title: Review Questions 1
summary: Practice problem: determining which member functions are called for processPerson with Person, Student, and CSStudent arguments.
main_text: Given a hierarchy: Person has virtual print_info() and non-virtual useComputer(). Student : public Person overrides print_info() and useComputer(). CSStudent : public Person overrides print_info() and useComputer(). void processPerson(Person* p) { p->print_info(); p->useComputer(); }. Questions: As we call processPerson(&p) what member functions will be called? As we call processPerson(&s)? As we call processPerson(&cs)? We use the terms static and dynamic binding when referring to which function will be called when virtual is NOT or IS present.
notes_text: Apply the 1-2-3 algorithm: pointer type is Person*. For print_info(): it is virtual in Person, so use dynamic binding (object type). For useComputer(): it is NOT virtual in Person, so use static binding (pointer type = Person).

title: Review Questions 2
summary: Practice questions about pure virtual functions, abstract classes, instantiation rules, and when to use virtual destructors.
main_text: Given Person with virtual print_info() = 0 and virtual useComputer(). Student : public Person overrides print_info(). CSStudent : public Student overrides print_info() and useComputer(). Questions: What does '= 0;' mean in the declarations? (Pure virtual function.) What do we call a class with 1 or more of these kind of declarations? (Abstract class.) Is it okay that Student doesn't provide a useComputer() implementation? (Yes, it inherits Person::useComputer().) Can we declare Person objects? Can we declare pointers or references to Person objects? When should a class have a virtual destructor?
notes_text: Key answers: = 0 means pure virtual, making the class abstract. Student inherits useComputer() from Person (which has an implementation since only print_info is pure virtual). Cannot declare Person objects (abstract), but CAN declare Person pointers/references. Virtual destructor needed when at least one other virtual function is declared.

title: Solutions - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing solutions to the review questions.
main_text: Solutions. This section provides the answers to the review questions.
notes_text: Students should attempt the review questions before looking at solutions.

title: Assignment of Base/Derived - Solution
summary: Confirms that derived-to-base assignment is valid (p = s) but base-to-derived is invalid (s = p), with memory layout explanation.
main_text: Can we assign a derived object into a base object? Can we assign a base object into a derived? Think hierarchy and animal classification: Can any dog be (assigned as) a mammal? Yes. Can any mammal be (assigned as) a dog? No. We can only assign a derived into a base (since the derived has EVERYTHING the base does). p = s (Base = Derived) is Good! s = p (Derived = Base) is Bad! The memory layout shows Person (name_, id_) can receive Student data (name_, id_ copied, major_ and gpa_ sliced off), but Student cannot receive Person data because major_ and gpa_ would be undefined.
notes_text: This is the solution slide for the type compatibility question. The arrow from Student to Person shows valid assignment direction, while the prohibition symbol shows the invalid direction.

title: Review Questions 1 - Solutions
summary: Provides solutions showing which functions are called for each processPerson call based on virtual/non-virtual status.
main_text: Person has virtual print_info() and non-virtual useComputer(). Student and CSStudent each override both. void processPerson(Person* p) { p->print_info(); p->useComputer(); }. Solutions: processPerson(&p): Person::print_info() (virtual, object is Person) / Person::useComputer() (not virtual, pointer type Person). processPerson(&s): Student::print_info() (virtual, object is Student) / Person::useComputer() (not virtual, pointer type Person). processPerson(&cs): CSStudent::print_info() (virtual, object is CSStudent) / Person::useComputer() (not virtual, pointer type Person). Static and dynamic binding terms refer to which function will be called when virtual is NOT or IS present.
notes_text: The pattern is clear: print_info is virtual so it uses dynamic binding (follows the object type). useComputer is NOT virtual so it always uses static binding (follows the pointer type, which is always Person*). This is why Person::useComputer() is called every time regardless of the actual object.

title: Review Questions 2 - Solutions
summary: Answers about pure virtuals, abstract classes, inheritance of virtual implementations, and virtual destructor rules.
main_text: Solutions: What does '= 0;' mean? Pure virtual function. What do we call such a class? Abstract class. Is it okay that Student doesn't provide a useComputer() implementation? Yes, it inherits Person::useComputer(). Can we declare Person objects? No (Person is abstract with print_info() = 0). Can we declare pointers or references to Person objects? Yes. When should a class have a virtual destructor? When at least one other virtual function is declared in the class.
notes_text: Critical distinctions: you cannot create objects of abstract types, but you CAN create pointers and references to them. This is essential for polymorphism - you need base pointers/references to enable dynamic dispatch, even when the base is abstract.

title: Polymorphism: As Easy as 1-2-3 - Solution
summary: Worked solution applying the 1-2-3 algorithm to a three-level hierarchy with mixed virtual and non-virtual functions.
main_text: Hierarchy: Person has virtual print_info() and non-virtual code(). Student : public Person has print_info(), virtual code(), and virtual study(). CSStudent : public Student has code() and study(). Objects: Person p("Bill",1); Student s("Jill",2,5); CSStudent cs("Cory",3,6). Person *q; Student* t;. q = &s; q->print_info() calls Student version (virtual in Person, object is Student). q->code() calls Person version (not virtual in Person, pointer type is Person). q = &cs; q->code() calls Person version (not virtual in Person, pointer type is Person). t = &cs; t->print_info() calls Student version (virtual in Student, object is CSStudent which inherits Student's). t->code() calls CSStudent version (virtual in Student, object is CSStudent).
notes_text: This comprehensive example shows why the 1-2-3 algorithm is essential. The same function (code()) behaves differently depending on which pointer type is used because virtual status differs at different levels. Through Person*, code() is static binding. Through Student*, code() is dynamic binding because Student declared it virtual.
